item.title: Students warned against post exam nuisance
item.description: Grade 10 and 12 students have been warned that public nuisance after the final examinations will not be tolerated. NCD Metropolitan Superintendent Warrick Simatab, in a statement issued today, warned students against alcohol and home brew consumption, drug use, noise pollution and school fights.
item.content:encoded:
Grade 10 and 12 students have been warned that public nuisance after the final examinations will not be tolerated.

NCD Metropolitan Superintendent Warrick Simatab, in a statement issued today, warned students against alcohol and home brew consumption, drug use, noise pollution and school fights.

“Be responsible. I will not tolerate public nuisance by students involved in alcohol, home brew, drugs, noise pollution, or school fights,” he said.

He reminded students that a precedent was set earlier this year when police arrested and charged 90 students over school fights.

“That precedent stands. I will not mince my words on this. Celebrate your achievement the right way, safely, and with respect for your community.”

Superintendent Simatab also urged parents to take responsibility for their children’s safety and behaviour during the post-exam period.

At the same time, he encouraged students sitting their final exams to remain focused.

“Stay focused, do your best, and make your families and this city proud.”

item.title: 109 grade 10 students miss national exams after Bareji violence
item.description: One hundred and nine Grade 10 students at Bareji High School in the Northern Province have been unable to sit their 2026 National Examinations following a deadly stabbing incident and subsequent violence at the school on Monday. Bareji High School is a boarding school located along the Afore Highway, on the border of Ijivitari and Popondetta districts.
item.content:encoded:
One hundred and nine Grade 10 students at Bareji High School in the Northern Province have been unable to sit their 2026 National Examinations following a deadly stabbing incident and subsequent violence at the school on Monday.

Bareji High School is a boarding school located along the Afore Highway, on the border of Ijivitari and Popondetta districts.

The National Examinations began on Monday, October 5, and will end on Friday, October 9.

The students did not sit their examinations after the stabbing incident resulted in a death, the burning of a dormitory and the destruction of school properties.

Head Teacher for Bareji High School, Moses Sari, says the incident stemmed from a relationship between two Grade 9 students, which the female student's mother disapproved of.

The mother allegedly pulled out a bush knife to stab the male student, but ended up stabbing her own daughter, leading to her death.

Following the death, relatives of the deceased female student retaliated and burned down a male dormitory and destroyed the school administration building, three staff houses and the school mess on Monday, October 5, 2026.

Mr Sari said the relatives were armed with guns, bush knives, spears and other weapons, and fired gunshots.

The deceased female student has been taken to the Popondetta Hospital morgue, while the suspect mother has been detained at the Popondetta police cell.

Teachers, students and parents fled the school, taking refuge in nearby bushes until daybreak.

They have since been moved out of the school premises as of Tuesday, October 6, 2026.

High and Secondary School Inspector Jess Jim says the school will remain "closed until the issue is ironed out".

PPC Northern Chief Inspector Charles Winuwan says the arson case suspects will be arrested soon with the help of community leaders from the Bareji area.

item.title: American cyclist travels across PNG by bicycle
item.description: American traveller Henry Hall is cycling across Papua New Guinea, combining road and boat travel as he explores the country before continuing his journey to Indonesia. Hall, who is from the United States and previously lived in Ireland, said his interest in Papua New Guinea began as a child after reading about the country and its cultural diversity.
item.content:encoded:
American traveller Henry Hall is cycling across Papua New Guinea, combining road and boat travel as he explores the country before continuing his journey to Indonesia.

Hall, who is from the United States and previously lived in Ireland, said his interest in Papua New Guinea began as a child after reading about the country and its cultural diversity.

He said PNG had always fascinated him, but the distance and cost of travelling to the country prevented him from visiting for many years.

Hall eventually decided to explore Papua New Guinea by bicycle after developing an interest in bicycle travel.

“I enjoy travelling by bicycle because of the experiences it offers, so I decided I would like to try cycling in Papua New Guinea,” he said.

He brought his bicycle from the United States and assembled it in Kavieng, New Ireland Province, before cycling south along the Buluminski Highway for five days.

From New Ireland, Hall travelled by boat to East New Britain, where he spent time cycling around Kokopo.

He later learned that the MV Karkar was departing Rabaul for Lae. As the vessel operates only about once a month, he quickly arranged his ticket and boarded.

The five-day voyage to Lae allowed Hall to witness traditional welcomes and celebrations at different ports along the way.

After arriving in Lae, he travelled up the highlands for several days, leaving his bicycle with people who kindly looked after it.

He later returned to Lae and resumed his cycling journey towards Madang, completing the trip in three days.

Hall said the journey gave him the opportunity to experience villages, landscapes, and communities along the route.

However, he said the final stretch into Madang was challenging because of the steep and rocky mountain terrain.

“I underestimated those mountains. They are steep and rocky, but I kept pushing,” he said.

Hall has spent several days in Madang resting and also participated in a bicycle race in town on September 12.

He said his next destination is Vanimo, from where he plans to continue his journey into Indonesia.

Hall said travelling through Papua New Guinea by bicycle had allowed him to experience the country and its people in a different way.

item.title: Kaintiba LLG faces El Nino effects
item.description: Kaintiba Local Level government area has also been hard hit by the effects of El nino at this time. According to the Kerema District youth council president, Japhet Yamando, safe drinking water has become scarce after water in the tanks dried up.
item.content:encoded:
Kaintiba Local Level government area has also been hard hit by the effects of El nino at this time.

According to the Kerema District youth council president, Japhet Yamando, safe drinking water has become scarce after water in the tanks dried up.

He said the people turned to the little creeks for drinking and cooking for many months until now these creeks have also dried up.

Yamando said the people are now drinking and cooking using water from the two big rivers locally known as Naguta and Na Nenemba.

He said the long dry spell has also affected food crops in the gardens which are dying affecting also domesticated animals as a result.

Apart from plants and animals little children have also been falling sick mainly with diarrhoea, as such parents have been made aware to boil the water and let it cool for consumption.

item.title: El Nino affects power supply
item.description: The Sirinumu Dam is now at 53 percent as El Nino continues to worsen putting pressure on water and electricity supply in Port Moresby. PNG Power Limited Chief Executive Officer, Paul Bayly said this follows the continuous load shedding that is happening in the city.
item.content:encoded:
The Sirinumu Dam is now at 53 percent as El Nino continues to worsen putting pressure on water and electricity supply in Port Moresby.

PNG Power Limited Chief Executive Officer, Paul Bayly said this follows the continuous load shedding that is happening in the city.

“More than half of our electricity generation supplied to Port Moresby and the Central province normally comes from hydroelectric generation. Sirinumu Dam is currently at 53% capacity.

"PNG power and Water PNG have already implemented measures to limit the water releases and to protect the essential water supply." Bayly said.

Bayly explains that reduced power releases have cut generation at the Rouna hydro stations from 40 MW to 24 MW, a 40% drop.

“Reduced water releases have lowered output from Rouna hydro stations from 40 MW capacity to 24 MW today.

“That's a reduction of 40%. Edevu hydro power station, which relies on the Brown River, has also reduced its generation from about 56 MW to 14 MW today. That's a reduction of 75%.

“Together, these sharp reductions demonstrate the severe impact that El Nino is having." He said.

He highlighted the steps of which PNG Power will take to ensure available power generation.

“PNG Power is also taking immediate steps to stabilize the grid and to increase available generation.

New Power has 56 MW of capacity while Dirio has 45 MW of capacity.

However, current transmission limitations restrict the amount that can be delivered from Dirio to just 30 MW. The PNG Power CEO says the decline in hydro generation shows the serious impact of El Nino on electricity supply and the reliability of the Port Moresby grid.

item.title: Secretary commends district for prioritizing education
item.description: Education Secretary Dr Uke Kombra commended the progress of construction work under Huon Gulf's education project when he recently visited the upcoming Wampar Secondary School site in the district. The new secondary school project currently involves the construction of four 6-in-1 duplex classrooms, 10 teachers' houses and two ablution blocks for a start.
item.content:encoded:
Education Secretary Dr Uke Kombra commended the progress of construction work under Huon Gulf's education project when he recently visited the upcoming Wampar Secondary School site in the district.

The new secondary school project currently involves the construction of four 6-in-1 duplex classrooms, 10 teachers' houses and two ablution blocks for a start.

Dr Kombra said he was impressed with what he saw on the ground.

"We are grateful that the district is prioritizing education to address the National Education Plan 1-6-6 Policy, and that no child must be left behind," Dr Kombra said.

Dr Kombra stressed that there are other requirements the district must also meet, including registration of the school, recruitment of teachers, and provision of proper learning resources. He said an official inspection will then be conducted to confirm if all requirements are fully met.

"Infrastructure is the biggest challenge of establishing a new school, but with the progress so far, the district must maintain the momentum to have it complete," he said.

Huon Gulf MP Jason Peter, during an event, said that Wampar Secondary School is one of his key initiatives.

item.title: ANG increase Buka capacity
item.description: The National Flag Carrier Air Niugini, has increased its passenger and cargo capacity, on its flights to and from Buka, in the Autonomous Region of Bougainville (AROB). Air Niugini Chief Executive Officer, Alan Milne in a statement says that this follows the opening of their new Jet A1 aviation fuel refueling facility, on the 30 th of September.
item.content:encoded:
The National Flag Carrier Air Niugini, has increased its passenger and cargo capacity, on its flights to and from Buka, in the Autonomous Region of Bougainville (AROB).

Air Niugini Chief Executive Officer, Alan Milne in a statement says that this follows the opening of their new Jet A1 aviation fuel refueling facility, on the 30 th of September.

Mr. Milne says that the facility, which is owned by Ok Tedi Energy, a subsidiary of Ok Tedi Mining Limited (OTML), will enable them to carry more passengers and cargo from Port Moresby to Buka and return, because they will now be able to refuel in Buka.

Mr. Milne also says that this is welcome news for the airline, because it improves aircraft efficiency, and it will further benefit communities and businesses, as they head into the festive period.

He also adds that a Fokker 100 was the first plane to refuel in Buka, when the facility was launched, and this saw them immediately clear a backlog of cargo from Port Moresby on that single flight.

Meanwhile, OTML Managing Director, Kedi Illimbit says, the project is part of Ok Tedi Energy’s push to strengthen PNG’s infrastructure, and provide fuel security and certainty.

item.title: Frieda River brings project information to West Sepik communities
item.description: Frieda River Limited has completed the first phase of its District Town Hall Engagements in West Sepik, taking information on the proposed Sepik Development Project directly to Local Level Governments and communities. The engagements covered Telefomin, Green River, Amanab, Vanimo town, Bewani and Maka Base in Walsa LLG, with government representatives also taking part.
item.content:encoded:
Frieda River Limited has completed the first phase of its District Town Hall Engagements in West Sepik, taking information on the proposed Sepik Development Project directly to Local Level Governments and communities.

The engagements covered Telefomin, Green River, Amanab, Vanimo town, Bewani and Maka Base in Walsa LLG, with government representatives also taking part.

The focus was to bring information about the project closer to the people and give communities an opportunity to hear from the project team, ask questions and understand where the development process currently stands.

For some elders, the discussions brought back memories of a project they first heard about when they were children, with the Frieda River Project having been under discussion in the Sepik region for more than 50 years.

FRL Country Manager Dr Joel Hamago said the long history of the project made direct engagement important, particularly for people who may not have had the opportunity to follow its development through formal processes.

He said the town halls were designed to allow communities to ask questions about the project's current stage, environmental requirements, proposed infrastructure and potential benefits and impacts.

The proposed Sepik Development Project includes the Frieda River copper-gold mine, hydroelectric power generation, a power transmission network, roads, pipelines, bridges, a proposed Green River Airport and Vanimo Ocean Port.

The project received six environmental permits from the Conservation and Environment Protection Authority in November 2025. The permits cover the proposed mine, hydroelectric project, power grid, infrastructure road, Green River Airport and Vanimo Ocean Port.

The project remains in the pre-development stage. Recent reporting has confirmed that construction is yet to begin and would proceed after the Special Mining Lease, or SML, is granted.

Dr Hamago told communities that FRL is now working through the requirements associated with the SML process and the next stages of project development.

Community questions during the town halls focused largely on employment, local business opportunities, landowner identification, benefit sharing and possible impacts on livelihoods and the environment.

Dr Hamago also explained the proposed Community Development Agreement, or CDA, including the distinction between direct and indirect benefits that could arise from the project.

He said a separate workshop would be organised for landowners and the wider public to provide more detailed information on the CDA process and how communities can participate.

The engagements were welcomed by communities, particularly the opportunity to receive information directly and ask questions about a project that could have long-term implications for the region.

The discussions also highlighted the importance of continued consultation as the project moves through its regulatory and development stages.

The second phase of the town hall program is expected to cover Aitape, Lumi, Yangkok and Nuku, extending the discussions to more communities across West Sepik.

The ongoing engagements will provide further opportunities for communities to understand the proposed project, while allowing project representatives to hear local concerns and expectations.
